[00:00:05] OK, let's get started.
[00:00:08] So today is the second day on data.
[00:00:13] Last time we talked about how data doesn't really
[00:00:16] just fall from the sky.
[00:00:18] You actually have to think about where it comes from.
[00:00:21] So in general, the internet consists of live services.
[00:00:27] That data on those services have to be either dumped or crawled.
[00:00:31] And then there's an additional step where
[00:00:33] you have to process the data.
[00:00:35] And we also talked about various societal considerations,
[00:00:42] terms of service, copyright.
[00:00:44] You have to either get a license or appeal to fair use.
[00:00:46] So there's a lot of complexity that goes into data.
[00:00:50] So today we're going to look more at the data pipeline
[00:00:54] from transforming the data, filtering the data,
[00:00:57] deduplication, and mixing.
[00:01:01] And then we're going to top it off
[00:01:02] by talking a bit about post-training data,
[00:01:07] in particular, how folks are using synthetic data these days.
[00:01:12] So the first part is going to be mostly about pre-training.
[00:01:15] That's what you should have in mind.
[00:01:18] So we talked a little bit about data transformation already,
[00:01:21] but just as a reminder.
[00:01:24] So raw data doesn't come as text, even as
[00:01:28] if you've scraped something.
[00:01:30] If you ever look inside Common Crawl, it's not text.
[00:01:34] It's either HTML.
[00:01:36] Sometimes it could be PDFs or directories
[00:01:39] in the case of GitHub.
[00:01:42] So most of the attention on transforming data
[00:01:47] is dealing with HTML because most of the web is in HTML.
[00:01:51] And for this processing, a lot of this is fairly heuristic.
[00:01:57] There's removing of boilerplate, like navigation and ads,
[00:02:02] and extracting content, which is the main part of the page.
[00:02:06] And there's some subtleties around what constitutes content.
[00:02:11] Usually, you get rid of the footers and headers, and maybe
[00:02:16] menus, and those things, and you try to extract the content.
[00:02:20] But you could imagine in cases where
[00:02:23] some of the navigation elements might
[00:02:26] be helpful to learn what web pages look like.
[00:02:28] So what is content and what is not content is not always clear.
[00:02:33] And then what do you do about images and tables that
[00:02:36] are in web pages?
[00:02:40] So inherently, this is a lossy process
[00:02:42] because you need to linearize HTML, which at least is
[00:02:46] either hierarchical or visual, if you
[00:02:48] think about the rendered output, and to a sequence of tokens.
[00:02:52] And particular tables are a bit tricky to deal with.
[00:02:56] Simple tables, you can render using markdown.
[00:03:00] But if you have nested tables, then that
[00:03:03] becomes quite challenging.
[00:03:05] You have to give up at some point
[00:03:08] or approximate at some point.
[00:03:11] So, typically, HTML to text processing is rule-based.
[00:03:16] And the reason for this is that rule-based processors
[00:03:21] are very fast.
[00:03:24] And also, you're not trying to do too much here.
[00:03:30] You don't need too much intelligence.
[00:03:31] So rule-based generally works.
[00:03:34] Now, I think there could be a case
[00:03:36] for model-based interventions at this point.
[00:03:40] They have to be very fast, and they
[00:03:41] have to do something more intelligent.
[00:03:46] But if you ever look at data, you'll
[00:03:48] notice there are imperfections in the data
[00:03:50] just because any rule-based processing have some failure
[00:03:56] rate.
[00:03:57] As we showed last time, the accuracy
[00:04:00] does matter, depending on which tool you choose.
[00:04:06] If you use Resiliparse or Trafilatura, then--
[00:04:08] I guess Resiliparse on these extended dclm evals
[00:04:15] works better than the others.
[00:04:20] I'll talk also briefly about PDFs.
[00:04:22] So there's Hugging Face work, which released
[00:04:26] a data set called FinePDFs.
[00:04:28] So PDF files, if you ever opened them up, not in a PDF reader,
[00:04:34] looks like this, and this needs to get rendered.
[00:04:40] So PDFs can be found on just web pages on the internet.
[00:04:45] And Common Crawl does have some PDFs.
[00:04:51] Generally, Common Crawl focuses on text,
[00:04:53] but sometimes, if you're just given a URL,
[00:04:56] you might not even know before you fetch it whether it's a PDF
[00:04:58] or not, if it doesn't have the extension.
[00:05:04] If you read this blog post, there's
[00:05:05] a lot of details, which I'll spare you of.
[00:05:09] For example, one thing is that many of the PDFs
[00:05:12] that are in Common Crawl are truncated because PDFs are big,
[00:05:16] so then that demands that recrawling is necessary.
[00:05:20] And then there's a question-- once you have the PDF file,
[00:05:22] how do you actually convert it to text?
[00:05:25] And, some PDFs might be just scans as well.
[00:05:28] So they're essentially images.
[00:05:30] So there's a bunch of tools that this paper tried out,
[00:05:36] but mostly this involves running OCR using a VLM.
[00:05:42] And this obviously can be much more expensive than what
[00:05:45] we were doing before with text.
[00:05:47] Fortunately or unfortunately, the PDFs
[00:05:51] are a very small fraction of the whole internet.
[00:05:54] But they are very valuable because generally,
[00:05:58] if you bother to make a PDF, that means you probably
[00:06:01] have something interesting to say as opposed to a web page.
[00:06:05] So the quality of an average PDF is generally higher
[00:06:10] than for HTML file.
[00:06:15] There's a lot of cleanup and filtering.
[00:06:17] And PDFs, more so even than web pages,
[00:06:21] a lot of layout information is missing,
[00:06:24] because in HTML you have various tags like h1 and p
[00:06:29] that gives you some semantic information.
[00:06:31] PDFs are, by design, all about layout.
[00:06:34] So you don't necessarily preserve the semantic structure.
[00:06:42] So there's a bunch of transformation that happens.
[00:06:45] At this point, you have text, but you're not done.
[00:06:53] You're far from done.
[00:06:54] So the next step is filtering.
[00:06:57] So I'm going to talk somewhat abstractly about what filtering
[00:07:01] is.
[00:07:02] Here's the building block.
[00:07:05] So suppose you have some target data that you want to get.
[00:07:10] This is usually a small amount of high-quality data and lots
[00:07:13] of raw data.
[00:07:15] This is the fresh shipment of the tokens
[00:07:20] that you transformed from the previous step.
[00:07:24] And the goal is to find a subset of this raw data that
[00:07:29] is similar to target.
[00:07:31] So this is the general skeleton for filtering,
[00:07:33] and almost all kinds of filtering
[00:07:36] falls into this schema.
[00:07:39] So filtering, there's many reasons
[00:07:41] you might want to filter.
[00:07:43] If you're training an English language
[00:07:45] model or a German language model,
[00:07:48] you might want to identify the language and filter things that
[00:07:51] don't match that language.
[00:07:53] The main reason for filtering is quality filtering.
[00:07:57] You want to find things that are high quality as opposed
[00:07:59] to low quality.
[00:08:00] You don't want just spam.
[00:08:02] You want encyclopedic information.
[00:08:07] And then another application is toxicity filtering.
[00:08:11] Of course, the internet has plenty of nasty content,
[00:08:14] and maybe you don't want to train your language
[00:08:16] model on that.
[00:08:19] So, for a filtering algorithm, you want some generalization
[00:08:24] from the target data, because you already
[00:08:27] have the target data.
[00:08:28] You don't want to only get the target data,
[00:08:31] but you also want it to be extremely fast
[00:08:35] because you have to run it on the whole internet.
[00:08:38] So this could be 100 trillion tokens worth of data.
[00:08:44] So generally, filtering is you end up
[00:08:47] with a very small fraction, a single-digit fraction
[00:08:49] of your entire data.
[00:08:54] OK.
[00:08:55] So remember the general framework
[00:08:56] given the target, and raw, you're trying to find a subset.
[00:09:02] So the general scheme is that you estimate some model based
[00:09:07] on R and T and derive a scoring function,
[00:09:10] and then you keep the examples in R based on their score.
[00:09:14] So typically, there are two types of classifiers.
[00:09:18] One are generative models.
[00:09:20] So this is basically you have your target data.
[00:09:25] You can just estimate a model of that data.
[00:09:31] And remember, this has to be cheap,
[00:09:33] so probably you're not training a big language model.
[00:09:36] Generally, KenLM basically says I'm going to train a 5-gram
[00:09:40] model.
[00:09:42] A more common thing, which I think
[00:09:44] we're mostly seeing these days, is just training a classifier.
[00:09:48] And the classifier says, I'm going
[00:09:51] to predict a positive label, for example,
[00:09:55] that are in T, my target, and negative labels
[00:09:59] for things that are in raw but not in T.

[00:10:03] So basically, it looks like T are your positive examples,
[00:10:09] some random subset of R are your negative examples.
[00:10:12] Maybe you balance it, and then you train a classifier.
[00:10:16] And the tool that people generally use
[00:10:18] is fastText because it's fast.
[00:10:21] And generally, it's just a linear classifier--
[00:10:24] a bag of words.
[00:10:26] And then once you have this model now
[00:10:28] for every new document, you can score it,
[00:10:31] and you set some appropriate threshold,
[00:10:33] depending on your quality bar, and you keep the examples.
[00:10:38] Sometimes stochastically, sometimes not.
[00:10:42] So this is very much a model-based filtering approach.
[00:10:47] Remember from the last lecture, there
[00:10:49] are many data sets from generally a few years ago
[00:10:53] that did not use model-based filtering because they wanted
[00:10:57] to not bias things too much.
[00:11:00] These days, I think basically everyone
[00:11:02] does some amount of model-based filtering
[00:11:05] because unless you are compute-plentiful, in which case
[00:11:11] you probably don't need to do as much filtering-- you can just
[00:11:14] train on everything.
[00:11:15] Most people are compute-poor.
[00:11:19] You have to be very smart about how you're filtering;
[00:11:21] otherwise, you're just wasting flops on low-quality content.
[00:11:27] OK, so let me talk through some instantiations of filtering.
[00:11:32] So remember, I mentioned language identification.
[00:11:36] So the goal is just to find-- given a piece of text,
[00:11:39] detect whether it's of a particular language.
[00:11:43] So Meta has trained this set of fastText language identification
[00:11:47] models, which often you can just use off the shelf.
[00:11:50] So it supports 176 different languages.
[00:11:53] It's been trained on a bunch of multilingual sites.
[00:11:56] So Wikipedia, remember, has a lot of languages.
[00:11:59] There's also translation sites and sites
[00:12:02] for different languages.
[00:12:03] So a language ID is generally a fairly easy problem
[00:12:09] compared to many other tasks that we're dealing
[00:12:12] with-- so a simple classifier.
[00:12:14] If you look at a few words, you can tell
[00:12:16] that it's Spanish or Japanese.
[00:12:19] Now, there are subtleties because of code-switching
[00:12:23] and text, and there's some dialects.
[00:12:25] So I wouldn't say it absolutely solved problem,
[00:12:29] but this is not really the bottleneck
[00:12:31] for training a good language model.
[00:12:35] And then you can just-- so once you have your classifier,
[00:12:38] you just choose some threshold.
[00:12:40] This is generally fairly heuristic.
[00:12:43] So another thing you can do with filtering is that,
[00:12:47] suppose you're looking for data of a certain type.
[00:12:50] So let's say you want to get really good at math,
[00:12:53] so you want to go and find a bunch of math data.
[00:12:55] So OpenMathText is this paper from 2023,
[00:13:01] where the goal is to create a large corpus of math text.
[00:13:05] This pipeline consists of a few steps.
[00:13:09] So it's not training a single classifier.
[00:13:11] So first, you use some rules to filter.
[00:13:13] Does it contain latex commands?
[00:13:16] They also use KenLM.
[00:13:18] So this is a generative approach.
[00:13:20] And trained it on the ProofPile, which
[00:13:22] is a known data set of math, and keep it
[00:13:26] if the perplexity is below some threshold.
[00:13:30] And then you also train a fastText classifier
[00:13:33] to predict whether it's mathematical writing or not.
[00:13:38] And there's two different thresholds
[00:13:41] if it has latex in it, then it's a higher bar--
[00:13:44] sorry-- it's a lower bar, but if it doesn't have latex in it,
[00:13:48] it's a higher bar.
[00:13:51] And then, as a result, they got 15 billion tokens,
[00:13:55] which they use to train models.
[00:13:58] And there's a paper that showed that this more targeted, curated
[00:14:01] data collection results in models
[00:14:03] that are better at math than models that were trained
[00:14:07] on 20 times as much data, which were not filtered in this way.
[00:14:13] So the quality filtering again, think about it as a tool.
[00:14:17] You can define quality however you want.
[00:14:20] There's no universal notion of quality.
[00:14:22] If you want to define quality to be math,
[00:14:24] then you can go and get math, and you get better at it.
[00:14:27] So GPT-3, I think I mentioned this last time,
[00:14:30] but just to put it in this framework.
[00:14:32] So positive examples are Wikipedia, WebText.
[00:14:36] So these are pages that link out from high-star Reddit posts,
[00:14:43] and some books.
[00:14:44] And negatives are generally sampled from the web.
[00:14:47] They train a linear classifier and keep documents
[00:14:50] if the linear classifier is scored highly enough.
[00:14:54] There's the first LLaMA paper.
[00:14:56] The positives were pages referenced by Wikipedia, not
[00:15:00] Wikipedia articles themselves.
[00:15:03] And it's this same idea.
[00:15:06] So phi-1 from Microsoft is interestingly also
[00:15:16] falls into this framework.
[00:15:17] So they started with-- the raw data is not already
[00:15:24] a Python subset of the stack.
[00:15:25] Remember this is all code.
[00:15:28] And they define a prompt, which determines educational value.
[00:15:38] And then they use GPT-4 to classify a subset of R,
[00:15:44] 100k subset of R with this prompt,
[00:15:50] and the ones that are positive are kept and called the target.
[00:15:55] So the target here is actually the output
[00:15:58] of an expensive classifier.
[00:16:02] And then you train a cheaper classifier,
[00:16:04] in their case, a Random Forest, but you could have probably
[00:16:06] used fastText as well.
[00:16:11] And then you select data that is classified positive
[00:16:15] by this classifier.
[00:16:17] And they also showed that using this data set,
[00:16:20] you do much better than if you're just using the raw data.
[00:16:26] So this performance goes up in fewer steps to a higher value.
[00:16:33] So toxicity works the same way.
[00:16:37] There's this Dataset--
[00:16:38] Jigsaw Toxic Comments, where it came from this project
[00:16:43] where the goal is to help people have better discussions online.
[00:16:46] So here the data is the Wikipedia talk pages, which can,
[00:16:51] I guess, for controversial sites get quite heated.
[00:16:55] And this has been annotated with whether there are
[00:16:58] any toxic comments on there.
[00:17:01] And you can similarly define positive and negative examples,
[00:17:04] and you can train a classifier on that.
[00:17:08] So now I think you have the tools, or some examples
[00:17:14] and inspiration.
[00:17:15] You can identify a particular type of data that you want.
[00:17:21] You build a classifier for it, and then you
[00:17:23] can go filter Common Crawl for that.
[00:17:26] I want to talk about one subtlety here,
[00:17:30] which is that-- no, the notion of what you want for data
[00:17:36] actually depends on what model you want to train.
[00:17:38] So in particular, it depends on the number
[00:17:40] of tokens you're training on.
[00:17:42] And so there's no optimal threshold.
[00:17:44] So before, when I looked at the classifier,
[00:17:47] it gives you a score.
[00:17:49] You can't say 0.9 and say that's the best because it
[00:17:52] depends on what you want to do.
[00:17:54] Intuitively, if you are going to train
[00:17:56] for a longer period of time, then you
[00:17:59] can tolerate lower quality data.
[00:18:02] If you're training for shorter, then you
[00:18:07] want higher quality data, in general.
[00:18:10] And of course, if you could wave a magic wand,
[00:18:16] if you're training for longer, you want more high-quality data,
[00:18:18] but that's not an option that you're given.
[00:18:21] The data pool is what it is.
[00:18:24] So here's a preliminary experiment
[00:18:30] that Michael Ryan did.
[00:18:32] So basically, this plot shows for a 157-million parameter
[00:18:36] model.
[00:18:37] We're taking a very small pool.
[00:18:40] So 100 works, which is a tiny fraction of Common Crawl.
[00:18:46] And we're training and training for more over time.
[00:18:54] So let's take a look at the blue curve.
[00:18:56] So the blue curve is dclm.
[00:18:58] And so the loss starts here.
[00:19:01] And then it comes down.
[00:19:03] And each of these lines is when you epoch over the data.
[00:19:08] So this is one epoch, and then the next blue
[00:19:10] is the second epoch, and so on and so forth.
[00:19:12] So there's not that much data.
[00:19:14] So eventually, you have to repeat your data.
[00:19:16] And the loss continues going down
[00:19:20] because the second time you look at the data,
[00:19:22] you're still learning things.
[00:19:24] And at some point, you start to overfit.
[00:19:29] Whereas if you look at Resiliparse,
[00:19:30] this is basically no filtering.
[00:19:33] So here, it's much worse in the beginning.
[00:19:37] But as you continue and continue, at some point,
[00:19:40] you also epoch.
[00:19:42] It starts to go down slower.
[00:19:45] So you see this trend where high-quality data
[00:19:49] is better in this regime, where you're not epoching.
[00:19:53] But once you get to lots and lots of tokens,
[00:19:57] high-quality data is no longer that great.

materials.title: def filtering (lines 60-144)
materials.text:
def filtering():
    text("Algorithmic building block:")
    text("- Given some **target data** T and lots of **raw data** R, find subset T' of R similar to T.")
    image("images/raw-target-schema.png", width=600)

    text("Applications:")
    text("- Language identification (English versus rest)")
    text("- Quality filtering (high quality versus low quality)")
    text("- Toxicity filtering (non-toxic versus toxic)")

    text("Desiderata for filtering algorithm:")
    text("- Generalize from the target data (want T and T' to be different)")
    text("- Extremely fast (have to run it on R, which is huge)")

    text("Survey paper on data selection "), link("https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.16827")

    text("General framework: Given target T and raw R, find subset of R similar to T")
    text("1. Estimate some model based on R and T and derive a scoring function")
    text("2. Keep examples in R based on their score")

    text("Types of classifiers:")
    text("- Generative model of T (KenLM): score(x) = p_T(x)")
    text("- Simple classifier (fastText): score(x) = p(T | x)")
    text("To use: keep examples x with score(x) >= threshold (stochastically)")

    text("Model-based filtering?")
    text("- Some deliberately do not use model-based filtering (C4, Gopher, RefinedWeb, FineWeb, Dolma)")
    text("- Some use model-based filtering (GPT-3, LLaMA, DCLM) [becoming the norm]")

    text("Language identification:")
    text("- Goal: find text of a specific language (e.g., English)")
    text("- fastText language identification "), article_link("https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/language-identification.html")
    text("- Off-the-shelf classifier")
    text("- Supports 176 languages")
    text("- Trained on multilingual sites: Wikipedia, Tatoeba (translation site) and SETimes (Southeast European news)")
    text("- Dolma keeps pages with p(English) >= 0.5 "), link(dolma_2024)

    text("OpenMathText "), link("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.06786")
    text("- Goal: curate large corpus of mathematical text from CommonCrawl")
    text("- Use rules to filter (e.g., contains latex commands)")
    text("- KenLM trained on ProofPile, keep if perplexity < 15000")
    text("- Trained fastText classifier to predict mathematical writing, threshold is 0.17 if math, 0.8 if no math")
    text("- Result: produced 14.7B tokens, used to train 1.4B models that do better than models trained on 20x data")

    text("GPT-3 "), link("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.14165")  # Appendix A
    text("- Positives: samples from {Wikipedia, WebText2, Books1, Books2}")
    text("- Negatives: samples from CommonCrawl")
    text("Train linear classifier based on word features "), article_link("https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/ml-features#tokenizer")
    text("Keep documents stochastically based on score")
    def keep_document(score: float) -> bool:

def jaccard_minhash():
    text("Let's now look at approximate set membership.")
    text("First we need a similarity measure.")

    text("### Jaccard similarity")
    text("Definition: Jaccard(A, B) = |A intersect B| / |A union B|")
    A = {"1", "2", "3", "4"}
    B = {"1", "2", "3", "5"}

    def compute_jaccard(A, B):
        intersection = len(A & B)  # @inspect intersection
        union = len(A | B)  # @inspect union
        return intersection / union
    jaccard = compute_jaccard(A, B)  # @inspect jaccard

    text("Definition: two documents are **near duplicates** if their Jaccard similarity >= threshold")

    text("Algorithmic challenge: find near duplicates in linear time")

    text("### MinHash")
    text("MinHash: a random hash function h so that Pr[h(A) = h(B)] = Jaccard(A, B)")

    text("Normally, you want different items to hash to different hashes")
    text("...but here, you want collision probability to depend on similarity")

    def minhash(S: set[str], seed: int):
        return min(mmh3.hash(x, seed) for x in S)

    text("Characteristic matrix representation:")
    text("item | A | B", verbatim=True)
    text("1    | 1 | 1", verbatim=True)
    text("2    | 1 | 1", verbatim=True)
    text("3    | 1 | 1", verbatim=True)
    text("4    | 1 | 0", verbatim=True)
    text("5    | 0 | 1", verbatim=True)

    text("Random hash function induces a permutation over items")
    text("Look at which item is first in A and which item is first in B.")
    text("Each item has the same probability as being first (min)")
    text("- If 1, 2, 3 is first, then first in A = first in B.")
    text("- If 4, 5 is first, then first in A ≠ first in B.")

    # Verify MinHash approximates Jaccard as advertised
    n = 100  # Generate this many random hash functions
    matches = [minhash(A, seed) == minhash(B, seed) for seed in range(n)]  # @stepover
    estimated_jaccard = len([m for m in matches if m]) / len(matches)  # @inspect estimated_jaccard
    assert abs(estimated_jaccard - jaccard) < 0.01

    text("Now we can hash our items, but a collision doesn't tell us Jaccard(A, B) > threshold.")

def locality_sensitive_hashing():
    text("Locality sensitive hashing (LSH) "), link(title="book chapter", url="http://infolab.stanford.edu/~ullman/mmds/ch3n.pdf")

    text("Suppose we hash examples with just one MinHash function")
    text("P[A and B collide] = Jaccard(A, B)")
    text("On average, more similar items will collide, but very stochastic...")

    text("Goal: have A and B collide if Jaccard(A, B) > threshold")
    text("We have to somehow sharpen the probabilities...")

    text("Solution: use n hash functions")
    text("Break up into b bands of r hash functions each (n = b * r)")

    n = 12      # Number of hash functions
    b = 3       # Number of bands
    r = 4       # Number of hash functions per band
    text("Hash functions:")
    text("h1 h2 h3 h4  |  h5 h6 h7 h8  |  h9 h10 h11 h12", verbatim=True)

    text("Key: A and B collide if for *some* band, *all* its hash functions return same value")
    text("As we will see, the and-or structure of the bands sharpens the threshold")

    text("Given Jaccard(A, B), what is the probability that A and B collide?")

    def get_prob_collision(sim, b, r):  # @inspect sim @inspect b @inspect r
        prob_match = sim ** r                        # Probability that a fixed band matches  @inspect prob_match
        prob_collision = 1 - (1 - prob_match) ** b   # Probability that some band matches  @inspect prob_collision
        return prob_collision

    text("**Example**")
    prob_collision = get_prob_collision(sim=0.8, b=5, r=10)  # @inspect prob_collision
    image("https://cdn.sanity.io/images/vr8gru94/production/b470799575b8e77911bacb8500977afef06d6c85-1280x720.png", width=600)


    sims = [0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.85, 0.9, 0.95, 0.98]
    probs = {sim: get_prob_collision(sim=sim, b=10, r=10) for sim in sims}  # @inspect probs @stepover

    probs = {sim: get_prob_collision(sim=sim, b=10, r=20) for sim in sims}  # @inspect probs @stepover

def data_mixing():
    text("Recall that language models are trained on multiple data sources.")

    text("Datasets in Marin: "), link(title="token viewer", url="https://huggingface.co/spaces/marin-community/token-count-viewer")
    image("images/marin-token-viewer.png", width=800)

    text("The Pile "), link(the_pile_2020)
    image("https://stanford-cs324.github.io/winter2022/lectures/images/the-pile.png", width=600)
    text("Key question: what distribution over the data sources should we use?")

    text("Example:")
    sources = {"Wikipedia", "CC", "GitHub"}
    p = {"Wikipedia": 0.3, "CC": 0.5, "GitHub": 0.2}  # One possible data mixture

    text("Baselines:")
    text("- Vibes: set p(s) manually based on intuition (quite common)")
    text("- Uniform sampling: sample uniformly (p(s) ∝ 1)")
    text("- Proportional mixing: sample proportional to the number of tokens in a source (p(s) ∝ num_tokens(s))")

    text("Intuition: should upweight higher quality sources")
    text("However...")
    text("1. We want to ensure diversity (e.g., across incomparable sources: literature, code, papers)")
    text("2. Each source is finite, so if put too much weight on a small source, then need to epoch over it")
    
    text("This last point is important and a bit subtle.")
    text("Example:")
    source_token_counts = {
        "low": trillion(10),  # 10T tokens (abundant) @stepover
        "high": billion(10),  # 10B tokens (scarce) @stepover
    }
    p = {"low": 0.5, "high": 0.5}  # Naive data mixture
    train_tokens = trillion(1)  # Train for 1T tokens @stepover
    low_num_epochs = (p["low"] * train_tokens) / source_token_counts["low"]  # @inspect low_num_epochs
    high_num_epochs = (p["high"] * train_tokens) / source_token_counts["high"]  # @inspect high_num_epochs
    text("50x epochs on high quality data...can lead to overfitting!")

    text("UniMax "), link("https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09151")
    text("- Setting: balancing different languages for multilingual models")
    text("- Previous work: between uniform and proportional mixing (p(s) ∝ num_tokens(s)^α for α in [0, 1])")
    text("- Idea: sample sources uniformly but with a hard **cap** C on number of epochs for any source")
    text("- Specifically, p(s) * num_training_tokens ≤ C for all sources s")

    text("Regression-based mixing "), link("https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01492"), link("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.12237")
    image("images/regmix.png", width=700)
    text("- Define distribution over mixtures `p` (e.g., Dirichlet) ")
    text("- Define regression method (e.g., linear, gradient boosted trees)")
    text("- Define target based on downstream evals (careful not to overfit!)")
    text("- Discrepancy between small and large scale (tradeoff cost and accuracy)")
    image("images/data-mixing-methods.png", width=700)
    text("Hope 1: regression model is accurate at minimizer 🙏")
    text("Hope 2: optimal data mixtures transfer from small to large scale 🙏")

    text("Hold on. There's at least one scale-dependent effect:")
    source_token_counts = {
        "low": trillion(10),  # 10T tokens (abundant) @stepover
        "high": billion(10),  # 10B tokens (scarce) @stepover
    }
    text("- If train small models on low token counts:")
    p = {"low": 0.1, "high": 0.9}  # More mass on high quality data
    text("- But if train large model on this mixture, we will epoch a ton on high quality data and overfit!")

    text("Simulated epoching "), link("https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.11747")
    text("- General idea: make small scale look like large scale (general theme of this course)")
    text("- Instantiation: downsample all sources proportionally")
    small_run_tokens = billion(10)  # @stepover
    large_run_tokens = trillion(1)  # @stepover
    ratio = small_run_tokens / large_run_tokens  # @inspect ratio
    downsampled_source_token_counts = {s: count * ratio for s, count in source_token_counts.items()}  # @inspect downsampled_source_token_counts
    text("- In this downsampled mixture, models that epoch too much won't look good.")
    text("- So the optimum will be more balanced.")
    p = {"low": 0.7, "high": 0.3}  # More mass on high quality data

    text("Summary:")
    text("- Problem: how to weight different data sources (e.g., Wikipedia, general, code)")
    text("- Regression-based mixing: estimate mixture → loss at small scale, optimize (analogous to scaling laws)")
    text("- Important consideration: epoching and overfitting (solution: cap or simulated)")
